ch29.title: The Hospital at Bethsaida
ch29.b001: A Tent City by the Sea, Summer A.D. 28
ch29.b002: From May 3 to October 3, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostolic party lived at the Zebedee home in Bethsaida, which had been greatly enlarged to hold the growing family of Jesus. Through all five months of the dry season an enormous camp stood on the shore nearby, its population ever changing—truth seekers, healing candidates, and the merely curious—numbering from five hundred to fifteen hundred. David Zebedee had general charge of this tented city, assisted by the Alpheus twins, and it was a model of order and sanitation. David managed it as a self-sustaining enterprise, yet no one was ever turned away. At least one day a week the apostles went fishing and sold their catch to David for the camp, turning the money over to the common treasury. In those five months several thousand came and went, from every part of the Roman Empire and from the lands east of the Euphrates. It was the longest settled and best-organized period of the Master’s teaching.
ch29.b003: Andrew remained in general charge of the apostolic work, while Peter had full charge of the school of the evangelists. Peter, James, and Andrew passed upon the applicants, and all the races and nationalities of the Roman world and the East, as far as India, were represented in this new school of the prophets. It ran on the plan of learning and doing. In the forenoon the apostles taught groups of students; in the afternoon the students taught the people by the seaside; after supper they talked over both. Each apostle taught his own view of the gospel. They made no effort to teach alike, and there was no standardized formulation of doctrine. Once a week Jesus presided at the question hour, unfailingly harmonizing their divergent views. Even so, Simon Peter tended to dominate the theology of the school, and next to him James Zebedee. From the hundred and more evangelists trained by the sea would come most of the later seventy. Among them was the nobleman’s son of Capernaum.
ch29.b005: A short distance south of the main tented city stood what should be regarded as the kingdom’s first hospital. Elman, a believing Syrian physician, with a corps of twenty-five young women and twelve men, conducted it for four months. The sick were separated according to their ailments and treated by all known material methods, together with the spiritual practices of prayer and faith encouragement.
ch29.b006: Jesus visited the sick not less than three times a week and made personal contact with each sufferer. About a thousand went away from the infirmary improved or cured, and as far as is known, no miracle of supernatural healing occurred among them. Yet the vast majority never ceased proclaiming that Jesus had healed them. Many of the cures did seem to resemble miracles, but they were such transformations of mind and spirit as may occur in expectant and faith-dominated persons under the influence of a strong, positive, and beneficent personality whose ministry banishes fear and destroys anxiety. Elman and his helpers tried to teach the sick the truth about the “possession of evil spirits,” but with little success; the belief that sickness was caused by an unclean spirit was well-nigh universal. In all his contact with the sick, Jesus did not disregard the instructions of his Paradise brother, Immanuel, given before the incarnation, concerning the techniques of treatment or the revelation of the unknown causes of disease. Still, those who ministered learned much by watching how he inspired faith and confidence in the suffering. The camp disbanded shortly before the season of chills and fever came on.
ch29.b008: In all these months Jesus conducted public services at the camp fewer than a dozen times. Not since his baptism had he been so much alone. Whenever one of the apostles ventured to ask why he was absent so often, he would answer that he was “about the Father’s business.” He had released Peter, James, and John to help train the evangelists, and so, whenever he went into the hills, he summoned any two apostles who were at liberty. In this way each of the twelve enjoyed close association with him.
ch29.b009: What he did in those solitary hours has not been revealed. It is inferred that the incarnated Sovereign of our universe was then in direct and executive association with many of his chief directors of universe affairs, and that the human Jesus chose to call such activities being “about his Father’s business.” Many times the two apostles who sat near him while he was alone for hours watched his features undergo rapid and multitudinous changes, though he spoke no word, and they saw no visible manifestation of celestial beings.
ch29.b011: Two evenings each week Jesus talked privately with any who wished, in a secluded corner of the Zebedee garden. One evening Thomas asked: “⟦Q 148:4.1⟧Why is it necessary for men to be born of the spirit in order to enter the kingdom? Is rebirth necessary to escape the control of the evil one? Master, what is evil?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus told him not to confuse evil with the evil one, the high administrator who had knowingly rebelled against the Father, and then set out the distinction:

ch29.b012.en: “Evil is the unconscious or unintended transgression of the divine law, the Father’s will.…

ch29.b013.en: “Sin is the conscious, knowing, and deliberate transgression of the divine law, the Father’s will.…

ch29.b014.en: “Iniquity is the willful, determined, and persistent transgression of the divine law, the Father’s will.”

ch29.b015: Mortal man, he explained, is subject to inherent evil tendencies, but such natural imperfections are neither sin nor iniquity. Thomas had been confused by the doctrines of the Greeks and the errors of the Persians, viewing mankind as beginning with a perfect Adam and rapidly degenerating. “⟦Q 148:4.8⟧Men are, indeed, by nature evil, but not necessarily sinful.⟦/Q⟧” Nor was man estranged from the Father, an alien or stepchild seeking legal adoption. “⟦Q 148:4.9⟧The Greeks and others have taught you that man is descending from godly perfection steadily down toward oblivion or destruction; I have come to show that man, by entrance into the kingdom, is ascending certainly and surely up to God and divine perfection.⟦/Q⟧” Thomas understood much of it, and as Jesus asked, he spoke to no one of this conversation until after the Master had left the world.
ch29.b016: At another of these interviews Nathaniel asked why the loving Father permitted so many of his children to suffer so many afflictions. Jesus answered that the natural order of this world had been upset many times by the sinful adventures of rebellious traitors, and that he had come to make a beginning of setting things in order. “⟦Q 148:5.3⟧But, my son, you should know that the Father does not purposely afflict his children.⟦/Q⟧” Then he said: “⟦Q 148:5.3⟧The Father does not send affliction as an arbitrary punishment for wrongdoing. The imperfections and handicaps of evil are inherent; the penalties of sin are inevitable; the destroying consequences of iniquity are inexorable.⟦/Q⟧” It was the Father’s will that man should work persistently toward the betterment of his estate on earth. Then he recited passage after passage Nathaniel might have found in the Scriptures had he read with discernment: “⟦Q 148:5.5⟧The Lord does not afflict willingly.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 148:5.5⟧He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 148:5.5⟧A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax he will not quench.⟦/Q⟧”
ch29.b018: That same evening John asked why so many apparently innocent people suffered so many diseases and afflictions. “My son,” Jesus answered, “⟦Q 148:6.2⟧you do not comprehend the meaning of adversity or the mission of suffering. Have you not read that masterpiece of Semitic literature—the Scripture story of the afflictions of Job?⟦/Q⟧” Job had been blessed with children, wealth, dignity, health, and everything men value, and the children of Abraham took such prosperity as sure evidence of divine favor. “⟦Q 148:6.2⟧But such material possessions and such temporal prosperity do not indicate God’s favor. My Father in heaven loves the poor just as much as the rich; he is no respecter of persons.⟦/Q⟧”
ch29.b019: He went through the counsel of Job’s three friends. Eliphaz told him that the wicked, not the righteous, suffer, and that he must deserve his punishment. Bildad, even more depressing, said that his children must have been sinners since they perished. Zophar admitted that God’s ways could not be understood and supposed there was some hidden purpose in his miseries. No wonder poor Job found little comfort. Failing to receive help from man, he was driven to God, and there followed the great struggle in his heart between faith and doubt, until at last his tortured soul rose to new heights of hope and uttered its cry of triumph, “My Vindicator lives!” Job, said Jesus, longed for a human God, a divine Being who knows man’s mortal estate. “⟦Q 148:6.7⟧Wherefore has the Son of Man come forth from the Father to live such a life in the flesh that he will be able to comfort and succor all those who must henceforth be called upon to endure the afflictions of Job.⟦/Q⟧”
ch29.b020: The Father, he added, does not reveal himself in the whirlwind but speaks within the human heart “⟦Q 148:6.10⟧as a still, small voice, saying, ‘This is the way; walk therein.’ Do you not comprehend that God dwells within you, that he has become what you are that he may make you what he is!⟦/Q⟧” And his final word was this: “⟦Q 148:6.11⟧The Father in heaven does not willingly afflict the children of men.⟦/Q⟧” Man suffers from the accidents of time and the imperfections of an immature existence, from the inevitable consequences of sin, and from the harvest of his own persistence in iniquity, “⟦Q 148:6.11⟧But man’s miseries are not a personal visitation of divine judgment.⟦/Q⟧” John pondered these sayings for many days. His whole afterlife was markedly changed by that conversation in the garden, though he never spoke of it until after the Master had gone.
ch29.b021: The Mason with the Withered Hand
ch29.b022: On the second Sabbath before the second preaching tour, Jesus spoke in the Capernaum synagogue on the “Joys of Righteous Living.” When he had finished, the maimed and sick crowded around him, and among them, as everywhere he went except into the hills, were the six spies from Jerusalem. Their leader induced a man with a withered hand to ask whether it would be lawful to be healed on the Sabbath. Jesus perceived that the man had been sent and asked him whether he would lift a sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath. The man answered: “⟦Q 148:7.2⟧Yes, Master, it would be lawful thus to do well on the Sabbath day.⟦/Q⟧” Then Jesus spoke to them all: “⟦Q 148:7.2⟧How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! I proclaim that it is lawful to do good to men on the Sabbath day.⟦/Q⟧” As they stood before him in silence, he said to the man: “⟦Q 148:7.2⟧Stand up here by my side that all may see you. And now that you may know that it is my Father’s will that you do good on the Sabbath day, if you have the faith to be healed, I bid you stretch out your hand.⟦/Q⟧” And as the man stretched it forth, it was made whole.
ch29.b023: The people were minded to turn on the Pharisees, but Jesus calmed them: “⟦Q 148:7.3⟧I have just told you that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, to save life, but I did not instruct you to do harm and give way to the desire to kill.⟦/Q⟧” The angry Pharisees hastened that very Sabbath to Tiberias to stir up Herod, but he refused to act and told them to carry their complaints to Jerusalem. This was the first miracle Jesus wrought in response to the challenge of his enemies, done not as a demonstration of power but as a protest against making the Sabbath a bondage of meaningless restrictions. The man, a stone mason named Aaron, returned to his work and lived a life of thanksgiving and righteousness.
ch29.b025: In the last week at Bethsaida word came that Abraham, a young and influential member of the Sanhedrin, had publicly espoused the teachings of Jesus and had been baptized by Abner in the pool of Siloam. All Jerusalem was agog, and messengers were dispatched to recall the six spies, three of whom had already been tremendously impressed by what they had seen. About the same time a trance prophet from Bagdad named Kirmeth disturbed the camp. Jesus allowed him freedom for a few days, but before he interceded, David Zebedee and a self-appointed committee had taken Kirmeth out into the lake, plunged him repeatedly into the water, and advised him to go and build a camp of his own. Abraham the Pharisee gave all his worldly goods to the apostolic treasury, which made possible the immediate sending forth of the hundred new evangelists.
ch29.b026: On Friday afternoon, October 1, Jesus held his last meeting with the apostles, evangelists, and leaders in the large front room of the Zebedee home, with the six Pharisees in the front row and the house entirely surrounded by a vast throng. A man long afflicted with paralysis had been carried from Capernaum on a small couch; he had talked with Aaron the mason and resolved to reach Jesus. His friends could not get through either door, so he had them procure ladders, loosen the tiles of the roof, and lower him by ropes until he lay on the floor before the Master. Jesus stopped speaking. “⟦Q 148:9.2⟧Master, I would not disturb your teaching,⟦/Q⟧” said the man, “⟦Q 148:9.2⟧but I am determined to be made whole.… I would be made whole that I might serve in the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Though his affliction had come from his own misspent life, Jesus, seeing his faith, said: “⟦Q 148:9.2⟧Son, fear not; your sins are forgiven. Your faith shall save you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch29.b027: The Pharisees and scribes began to say within themselves, “⟦Q 148:9.3⟧Who can forgive sin but God?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus, perceiving their thoughts, said: “⟦Q 148:9.3⟧But that you who witness all this may finally know that the Son of Man has authority and power on earth to forgive sins, I will say to this afflicted man, Arise, take up your bed, and go to your own house.⟦/Q⟧” The paralytic arose, and as they made way for him, he walked out before them all. Many prayed and glorified God, saying they had never seen such things. Just then the messengers of the Sanhedrin arrived. After earnest debate the leader of the spies and two others returned to Jerusalem, while the other three confessed faith in Jesus, went straight down to the lake, and were baptized by Peter.
ch30.title: The Women Join the Work
ch30.b002: The second public preaching tour of Galilee began on Sunday, October 3, A.D. 28, and this time the 117 evangelists trained at Bethsaida went out with Jesus and the twelve. Before they left that morning, Andrew and Peter asked the Master to give the final charge to the new evangelists, but he declined, saying it was not his province to do what others could acceptably perform. James Zebedee gave the charge instead, and at its close Jesus said only: “⟦Q 149:0.2⟧Go now forth to do the work as you have been charged, and later on, when you have shown yourselves competent and faithful, I will ordain you to preach the gospel of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” For almost three months Peter and the other apostles each led about a dozen evangelists through Gadara, Ptolemais, Megiddo, Scythopolis, Gamala, and many other towns, while Jesus traveled with James and John alone, often visiting two cities in one day to watch and encourage the work. At Bethsaida, David Zebedee kept a permanent headquarters in his father’s house and employed forty to fifty messengers to carry news between the scattered workers.
ch30.b003: By now the fame of Jesus as a healer had spread through all Palestine, Syria, and the surrounding lands. On this tour he deliberately performed no so-called miracles. Yet there began to appear a peculiar and unexplained series of healings. More than a hundred men, women, and children from Judea, Idumea, Galilee, Syria, Tyre, Sidon, and beyond the Jordan were healed without Jesus’ conscious intent, and every time he observed such a case he charged the person to “tell no man.” He never explained these healings, except that on several occasions he said, “⟦Q 149:1.3⟧I perceive that power has gone forth from me,⟦/Q⟧” and once, when touched by an ailing child, “⟦Q 149:1.3⟧I perceive that life has gone forth from me.⟦/Q⟧” Those who recorded these things held that three influences worked together: the strong, living faith of the one who sought healing; the great compassion of the incarnated Creator Son; and the Father’s will—for what the Creator Son desires and the eternal Father wills IS. Others sought healing for selfish ends. A rich widow of Tyre followed him through Galilee with her retinue, offering more and more money, as if the power of God could be purchased by the highest bidder. She never became interested in the gospel at all.
ch30.b005: Jesus did little public work on this tour, but in most places where he stayed he held evening classes with the believers. When a young evangelist asked about anger, he said that it represents the measure of the failure of the spiritual nature to gain control of the intellectual and physical natures. “⟦Q 149:4.2⟧Anger depletes the health, debases the mind, and handicaps the spirit teacher of man’s soul.⟦/Q⟧” And he concluded: “⟦Q 149:4.2⟧Let your hearts be so dominated by love that your spirit guide will have little trouble in delivering you from the tendency to give vent to those outbursts of animal anger which are inconsistent with the status of divine sonship.⟦/Q⟧” On the same occasion he spoke of well-balanced character. Any virtue, carried to extremes, may become a vice: overmuch sympathy may degenerate into emotional instability, enthusiasm into fanaticism, courage into recklessness, prudence into cowardice. He pleaded for sympathy without sentimentality and piety without sanctimoniousness. What impressed his associates was not so much the teaching as the fact that his own life exemplified it. He lived in the midst of stress and storm, but he never wavered.
ch30.b006: Among the evangelists working under Simon Zelotes, Simon asked why some persons were so much happier than others. Much, Jesus said, depends upon a man’s willingness to be led by the Father’s spirit within him, and he quoted the wise man: “⟦Q 149:5.2⟧Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fatted ox and hatred therewith.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 149:5.3⟧Much of man’s sorrow is born of the disappointment of his ambitions and the wounding of his pride.⟦/Q⟧” Having sincerely done their best, men should cheerfully accept their lot and make the most of what has fallen to their hands. Jesus hardly regarded this world as a “vale of tears.” He looked upon it rather as the birth sphere of the eternal spirits of Paradise ascension, the “vale of soul making.”
ch30.b007: At Gamala Philip asked how to harmonize the Scriptures’ command to “fear the Lord” with the Master’s teaching that they should look to the Father without fear. “In the beginning,” Jesus answered, “⟦Q 149:6.2⟧it was only through fear that man could learn reverence, but I have come to reveal the Father’s love.⟦/Q⟧” From fear, through awe and reverence, he would lead them up to love. “⟦Q 149:6.7⟧Your fathers were taught to ‘fear God—the Almighty King.’ I teach you, ‘Love God—the all-merciful Father.’⟦/Q⟧” And he added: “⟦Q 149:6.8⟧In the kingdom of heaven, which I have come to declare, there is no high and mighty king; this kingdom is a divine family.⟦/Q⟧”
ch30.b008: By supper time on Thursday, December 30, a rainy day, all the apostles and evangelists had returned to the Zebedee home. Of the 117 who had gone out, only about seventy-five survived the test of actual experience and were on hand for further service.
ch30.b010: Of all the daring things Jesus did in his earth career, the most amazing was his sudden announcement on the evening of January 16, A.D. 29: “⟦Q 150:1.1⟧On the morrow we will set apart ten women for the ministering work of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” It was a day when a man was not supposed to salute even his own wife in a public place, when women were confined to the gallery of the synagogue, and when rabbis taught that it was “⟦Q 149:2.8⟧better that the words of the law should be burned than delivered to women.⟦/Q⟧”
ch30.b011: During the furlough Jesus had David send for ten devout women who had served in the former encampment and the tented infirmary. They had listened to the instruction given the young evangelists, but it had never occurred to them or their teachers that Jesus would dare to commission women to teach the gospel. They were Susanna, daughter of the former chazan of the Nazareth synagogue; Joanna, wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas; Elizabeth, daughter of a wealthy Jew of Tiberias and Sepphoris; Martha, elder sister of Andrew and Peter; Rachel, sister-in-law of Jude, the Master’s brother; Nasanta, daughter of Elman the physician; Milcha, a cousin of Thomas; Ruth, eldest daughter of Matthew Levi; Celta, daughter of a Roman centurion; and Agaman, a widow of Damascus. Later Jesus added Mary Magdalene and Rebecca, daughter of Joseph of Arimathea.
ch30.b012: The women organized themselves, choosing Susanna as their chief and Joanna as treasurer. Judas provided funds for their equipment and pack animals, but from then on they furnished their own support. Even the twelve were shocked. They had often heard the Master say that “⟦Q 150:1.3⟧in the kingdom of heaven there is neither rich nor poor, free nor bond, male nor female, all are equally the sons and daughters of God,⟦/Q⟧” yet they were literally stunned when he formally commissioned these women as religious teachers and let them travel with the party. The whole country was stirred, and the enemies of Jesus made great capital of it, but everywhere the women believers stood stanchly behind their chosen sisters. The charge Jesus gave them was the emancipation proclamation which set free all women for all time. The apostles practiced it after the Master’s departure, though later generations fell back into the olden customs.
ch30.b014: On Tuesday, January 18, about seventy-five tested evangelists joined the twenty-four, and the third tour began, lasting seven weeks. The evangelists went out in groups of five. As the party traveled, the women walked in the rear, and at conferences they sat together in front and to the right of the speaker. It was at Magdala that they first proved the wisdom of their choosing. Andrew had imposed strict rules on his associates about personal work with women of questionable character, but the women evangelists were free to enter the evil resorts and preach the glad tidings directly to all who lived there. Through their ministry Mary Magdalene was won for the kingdom. A succession of misfortunes, and the attitude of reputable society toward women who commit such errors of judgment, had brought her to one of the nefarious resorts of Magdala. It was Martha and Rachel who made plain to her that the doors of the kingdom were open even to such as she. Mary believed, and the next day Peter baptized her. She became the most effective teacher of the gospel among the twelve women. And when the last tragic episode of the Master’s life was enacted, though the apostles all fled but one, these women were all present, and not one either denied or betrayed him.
ch30.b015: At Tiberias, on Jesus’ instructions, the Sabbath services were placed in the hands of the women. Joanna led the meeting in the banquet room of Herod’s new palace, Herod being away, and read from the Scriptures about Miriam, Deborah, Esther, and other women of Israel. Late that evening, because a bright and supposedly new star had recently been seen, Andrew asked whether it signified the birth of a great man. Jesus answered with a thoroughgoing discussion of superstition. The courses of the stars have nothing to do with human life; astrology has no place in the gospel. The organs of a slain animal reveal nothing of the future. The spirits of the dead do not come back to communicate with the living. Charms and relics are impotent; casting lots does not disclose the divine will; the belief in magic numbers and omens is pure superstition; idols are nothing more than the material of which they are made. The only means of communion with the spiritual world is the spirit endowment of mankind—the indwelling spirit of the Father, the outpoured spirit of the Son, and the influence of the Infinite Spirit.
ch30.b017: The next evening Jesus gathered the apostles, John’s apostles, and the women. “⟦Q 150:4.1⟧You see for yourselves that the harvest is plenteous, but the laborers are few.⟦/Q⟧” He would stay with the younger teachers and send the older ones out two and two: Andrew and Peter, James and John Zebedee, Philip and Nathaniel, Thomas and Matthew, James and Judas Alpheus, Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot. “⟦Q 150:4.2⟧On this mission go not to any city of the gentiles, neither go into Samaria, but go instead to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.⟦/Q⟧” They were not to fear: “⟦Q 150:4.3⟧Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And yet I declare that not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.… Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than a great many sparrows.⟦/Q⟧” But peace would not always attend their preaching; when some of a family received the gospel and others rejected it, division and sorrow would follow. They did not come together again until the appointed meeting at Nazareth.
ch30.b018: One evening at Shunem, as Jesus taught a group of younger evangelists together with the women, Rachel asked: “⟦Q 150:5.1⟧Master, what shall we answer when women ask us, What shall I do to be saved?⟦/Q⟧” He answered: “⟦Q 150:5.2⟧Believe this gospel of the kingdom; accept divine forgiveness. By faith recognize the indwelling spirit of God, whose acceptance makes you a son of God.⟦/Q⟧” Entrance into the Father’s kingdom is wholly free, but growth in grace is essential to continuance in it. And he summed it up: “⟦Q 150:5.5⟧You cannot buy salvation; you cannot earn righteousness. Salvation is the gift of God, and righteousness is the natural fruit of the spirit-born life of sonship in the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” There was great rejoicing among those who heard, and the women rejoiced all the more to know they were included in these plans for the kingdom on earth.
ch30.b020: On Friday, March 4, the whole company gathered at an encampment on the highlands north of Nazareth. It was the first time Jesus had visited his home town since his public ministry began. That afternoon he walked about Nazareth unobserved and unrecognized. He passed the home of his childhood and the carpenter shop, and spent half an hour on the hill he had so loved as a lad. Not since his baptism in the Jordan had such a flood of human emotion stirred within his soul. Coming down from the hill, he heard the trumpet announcing the going down of the sun, just as he had heard it so many times as a boy, and he walked by the synagogue where he had gone to school.
ch30.b021: Nazareth did not welcome him. Most of his older friends, including the doting chazan teacher of his youth, were dead or gone, and the younger generation resented his fame with strong jealousy. The townspeople were offended that he had never included his native village in his tours and had done none of his great works there. His enemies had hired rough men to make trouble.
ch30.b022: The Sabbath was a beautiful day, and all Nazareth, friends and foes, crowded into the synagogue. The service ran just as it had when Jesus was a boy. When the chazan handed him the roll, no one seemed to recall that it was the very manuscript he himself had once presented to the synagogue. He read from Deuteronomy that the commandment is not in heaven nor beyond the sea, but “⟦Q 150:8.8⟧the word of life is very near to you, even in your presence and in your heart.⟦/Q⟧” Then he turned to Isaiah:

ch30.b023.en: “The spirit of the Lord is upon me because he has anointed me to preach good tidings to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and the recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are bruised and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.”

ch30.b024: He closed the book, sat down, and began: “Today are these Scriptures fulfilled.” For almost fifteen minutes he spoke on “⟦Q 150:1.3⟧The Sons and Daughters of God,⟦/Q⟧” and many marveled at his graciousness and wisdom.
ch30.b025: At the Edge of the Cliff
ch30.b026: When the service ended, Jesus stepped down into the crowd to answer questions, as was the custom. Many were bent on mischief, and the hired men circulated at the fringe. To their rude questions he answered half humorously: “⟦Q 150:9.1⟧Yes, I am Joseph’s son; I am the carpenter, and I am not surprised that you remind me of the proverb, ‘Physician heal yourself,’ … but I call you to witness that even the Scriptures declare that ‘a prophet is not without honor save in his own country and among his own people.’⟦/Q⟧” They jostled him and pointed their fingers: his brother was a common workman, his sisters still lived among them, and he did no wonders when he came back. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 150:9.2⟧I love the people who dwell in the city where I grew up, and I would rejoice to see you all enter the kingdom of heaven, but the doing of the works of God is not for me to determine. The transformations of grace are wrought in response to the living faith of those who are the beneficiaries.⟦/Q⟧”
ch30.b027: He would have good-naturedly managed the crowd, had not Simon Zelotes, with Nahor, one of the younger evangelists, gathered a group of friends and belligerently ordered the Master’s enemies to leave. His followers could not bear to see their beloved teacher treated with such disdain, and their vehement resentment only aroused the mob. Led by the hirelings, the ruffians seized Jesus, rushed him out of the synagogue to the brow of a near-by precipitous hill, and were about to shove him over the edge. Just then Jesus turned suddenly and faced his captors, quietly folding his arms. He said nothing. But as he started to walk forward, the mob parted, and he passed through unmolested.
ch30.b028: They left Nazareth the next morning. By noon on Thursday, March 10, all had reassembled at Bethsaida—not as an all-conquering band of triumphant crusaders, but as a sober and serious group of disillusioned preachers of the gospel of truth. They were beginning to realize that the kingdom would come only through much sorrow and bitter disappointment.
ch31.title: Parables by the Sea
ch31.b002: By March 10 all the preaching groups had gathered again at Bethsaida. Jesus spent most of the Sabbath day alone in the hills. That Saturday night he talked for more than an hour to the assembled company on “⟦Q 151:0.1⟧The mission of adversity and the spiritual value of disappointment.⟦/Q⟧” His hearers never forgot the lesson.
ch31.b003: He had not fully recovered from the sorrow of his rejection at Nazareth, and the apostles noticed a peculiar sadness mingled with his usual cheerfulness. In the weeks of waiting before the Passover, the women went from house to house in Capernaum and the surrounding villages, teaching the gospel and ministering to the sick.
ch31.b005: Because Jesus had talked with them far into the night, very few were up for breakfast on Sunday morning. He went down to the shore alone and sat in the old fishing boat of Andrew and Peter, always kept at his disposal, to meditate on the next move in the work of the kingdom. He was not alone for long. The people of Capernaum and the near-by villages began to arrive, and by ten o’clock almost a thousand were gathered on the beach near the boat, clamoring for his attention.
ch31.b006: Peter, now awake, came down to the boat. “⟦Q 151:1.1⟧Master, shall I talk to them?⟦/Q⟧” But Jesus answered, “⟦Q 151:1.1⟧No, Peter, I will tell them a story.⟦/Q⟧” He took the elevated seat in the boat, for it was the custom to sit when teaching, and while the small waves lapped against the hull, he spoke to the crowd along the shore:

ch31.b007.en: “A sower went forth to sow, and it came to pass as he sowed that some seed fell by the wayside to be trodden underfoot and devoured by the birds of heaven. Other seed fell upon the rocky places where there was little earth, and immediately it sprang up because there was no depth to the soil, but as soon as the sun shone, it withered because it had no root whereby to secure moisture. Other seed fell among the thorns, and as the thorns grew up, it was choked so that it yielded no grain. Still other seed fell upon good ground and, growing, yielded, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold.”

ch31.b008: When he had finished, he said to the multitude, “⟦Q 151:1.2⟧He who has ears to hear, let him hear.⟦/Q⟧” It was one of the first of a long series of parables; about this time Jesus first began to teach the multitudes in this way.
ch31.b010: The apostles were greatly perplexed. That evening in the Zebedee garden Matthew asked: “⟦Q 151:1.3⟧Master, what is the meaning of the dark sayings which you present to the multitude? Why do you speak in parables to those who seek the truth?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered that to them it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but to the undiscerning multitudes and to those who sought their destruction, the mysteries would now be presented in parables, so that those who really desired to enter the kingdom might discern the meaning, while those who listened only to ensnare them would hear without hearing. “⟦Q 151:1.4⟧My children, do you not perceive the law of the spirit which decrees that to him who has shall be given so that he shall have an abundance; but from him who has not shall be taken away even that which he has.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b011: The apostles did not fully grasp his meaning. While Andrew and Thomas talked further with Jesus, Peter and the others withdrew to another part of the garden and argued long and earnestly. They concluded that the parable was an allegory in which every feature had a hidden meaning, and Peter came to ask for an explanation. Jesus first asked for theirs. Peter said that the sower was the gospel preacher and the seed the word of God, and that the birds which snatched away the seed represented Satan, or the evil one. Then Nathaniel spoke. While he recognized many good things in Peter’s interpretation, he did not fully agree: to him the birds of the sky represented “⟦Q 151:2.3⟧one’s habits of life, the temptation of evil, and the desires of the flesh.⟦/Q⟧” The company fell into serious debate, almost equally divided, while Peter and Nathaniel withdrew to the house, each determined to change the other’s mind.
ch31.b012: The Master let the confusion pass its most intense point. Then he clapped his hands and called them about him. “⟦Q 151:2.5⟧Before I tell you about this parable, do any of you have aught to say?⟦/Q⟧” After a moment of silence, Thomas spoke. He reminded them that the Master had once taught them, when using illustrations, to choose a story best suited to one central and vital truth, and not to make a spiritual application of all the minor details. “That I am right,” he said, “⟦Q 151:2.5⟧is fully proved by the fact that, whereas we were all of one mind an hour ago, now are we divided into two separate groups.⟦/Q⟧” Andrew asked to hear Thomas’s own meaning, and Thomas said the parable taught one great truth: that their teaching of the gospel, however faithfully done, would meet with varying degrees of success, and that such differences were due to conditions in the circumstances of their ministry, “⟦Q 151:2.6⟧conditions over which we have little or no control.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b013: As Peter and Nathaniel were already on their way over to speak with Thomas, Jesus arose and said: “⟦Q 151:2.7⟧Well done, Thomas; you have discerned the true meaning of parables; but both Peter and Nathaniel have done you all equal good in that they have so fully shown the danger of undertaking to make an allegory out of my parables.⟦/Q⟧” The tension eased. Peter and Nathaniel congratulated each other on their interpretations, and before they retired for the night every apostle except the Alpheus twins ventured an interpretation of his own. Even Judas Iscariot offered a very plausible one.
ch31.b015: The apostles were now so parable-minded that the whole next evening was given to the subject. “My beloved,” Jesus began, “⟦Q 151:3.1⟧you must always make a difference in teaching so as to suit your presentation of truth to the minds and hearts before you.⟦/Q⟧” Before a multitude of varying intellects and temperaments one could not speak different words to each hearer, but one could tell a story, and each would interpret it according to his own endowments. “⟦Q 151:3.1⟧No man, when he lights a lamp, covers it up with a vessel or puts it under the bed.… Think not only of the multitudes and how they hear the truth; take heed also to yourselves how you hear.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b016: He advised against fables and allegories, but recommended the free use of parables, especially nature parables, and he spoke of the natural as “⟦Q 151:3.3⟧the unreal and fleeting shadow of spirit realities.⟦/Q⟧” A parable appeals at once to vastly different levels of mind and spirit. It proceeds from the known to the unknown, uses the material to introduce the spiritual, and evades much prejudice, putting new truth gracefully into the mind with a minimum of personal resentment. It avoids clashing with tradition and established authority, and it stirs the memory whenever the same scenes are met again. The appeal to nature also refuted the Jerusalem leaders’ claim that his work was done by the help of demons.
ch31.b017: Before dismissing them, he told them the last of the parable of the sower:

ch31.b018.en: “The kingdom of heaven is also like a man who cast good seed upon the earth; and while he slept by night and went about his business by day, the seed sprang up and grew, and although he knew not how it came about, the plant came to fruit. First there was the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And then when the grain was ripe, he put forth the sickle, and the harvest was finished.”

ch31.b019: Many times the apostles turned this saying over in their minds, but the Master never mentioned it again.
ch31.b020: The next day he taught again from the boat. An enemy sowed weeds among a man’s wheat, yet the householder told his servants to let both grow together until harvest, lest they uproot the wheat. The kingdom of heaven was like a grain of mustard seed, least of seeds, which grows until the birds of heaven rest in its branches; like leaven hidden in three measures of meal; like a treasure hidden in a field; like a merchant who sold everything to buy one pearl of great price; like a sweep net that gathers every kind of fish. From this time forward he seldom taught the masses except by parables, and in the evening classes he expounded his teaching more fully to the apostles and the evangelists.
ch31.b022: The multitude grew all through the week. On the Sabbath Jesus slipped away to the hills, but on Sunday the crowds returned. When he had spoken to them in the early afternoon, he said to his apostles: “⟦Q 151:5.1⟧I am weary of the throngs; let us cross over to the other side that we may rest for a day.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b023: On the way across they met one of those violent, sudden windstorms characteristic of the Sea of Galilee. The lake lies almost seven hundred feet below sea level, and after sunset the cooling air of the gorges tends to rush down upon it. Three boats of younger evangelists were trailing behind. The wind tore the sail away before they could furl it, and the waves began to wash over the side. It was one of the worst gales these experienced oarsmen had ever met, and they pulled hard for the shore, a little more than a mile and a half away.
ch31.b024: Jesus lay asleep in the stern under a small overhead shelter, for he was weary. When it began to fill with water, Peter dropped his oar, rushed to him, and shook him awake. “⟦Q 151:5.4⟧Master, don’t you know we are in a violent storm? If you do not save us, we will all perish.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus came out into the rain. He looked first at Peter, then peered into the darkness at the struggling oarsmen, and then turned back to Peter, who had not yet returned to his oar. “⟦Q 151:5.5⟧Why are all of you so filled with fear? Where is your faith? Peace, be quiet.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b025: He had hardly uttered these words when the disturbed atmosphere settled into a great calm. The angry waves subsided, the dark clouds spent themselves in a short shower and vanished, and the stars shone overhead. As far as can be judged, all this was purely coincidental. Jesus plainly explained that he had spoken to their troubled spirits and fear-tossed minds, not commanded the elements, but it was of no avail. From then on the apostles insisted that the Master had absolute power over the natural elements. Peter never grew weary of reciting how “⟦Q 151:5.6⟧even the winds and the waves obey him.⟦/Q⟧” The night was calm and beautiful, and they rested in the boats until sunrise.
ch31.b027: When they had gathered, about forty in all, Jesus pointed up a steep hillside. “⟦Q 151:6.1⟧Let us go up on this hillside for our breakfast and under some of the shelters rest and talk.⟦/Q⟧” The whole slope was honeycombed with caverns hewn out of the rock, many of them ancient sepulchres, and halfway up lay the cemetery of the little village of Kheresa. As they passed it, a lunatic who lived among the caverns rushed toward them. He had once been bound with fetters and chains in one of the grottoes, but long ago he had broken his shackles.
ch31.b028: His name was Amos, and he suffered from a periodic form of insanity. During one lucid interval he had gone to Bethsaida, heard Jesus and the apostles preach, and become a halfhearted believer. But a stormy phase soon returned, and he fled to the tombs, where he moaned and cried aloud and terrified all who met him. Now, recognizing Jesus, he fell at his feet. “⟦Q 151:6.4⟧I know you, Jesus, but I am possessed of many devils, and I beseech that you will not torment me.⟦/Q⟧” He truly believed that unclean spirits entered him at such times. In fact his troubles were mostly emotional; his brain was not grossly diseased.
ch31.b029: Jesus looked down at the man crouching like an animal at his feet, took him by the hand, and stood him up. “⟦Q 151:6.5⟧Amos, you are not possessed of a devil; you have already heard the good news that you are a son of God. I command you to come out of this spell.⟦/Q⟧” At once Amos was restored to his right mind and the normal control of his emotions. Villagers and swine herders gathered and were astonished to see him sitting with Jesus, freely conversing. As the herders rushed off to spread the news, dogs charged upon a small, untended herd of about thirty swine and drove most of them over a precipice into the sea.
ch31.b030: From this incidental occurrence arose the legend that Jesus had cast a legion of devils out of Amos and that the devils had entered the swine. Amos believed it too, for he had seen the swine tumbling over the brow of the hill just after his mind grew quiet, and this belief had a good deal to do with the permanence of his cure. All the apostles except Thomas believed it as well. Jesus did not get his rest; he was thronged all that day, and early Tuesday morning a delegation of the swine-raising gentiles came to Peter and Andrew: “⟦Q 151:6.7⟧Fishermen of Galilee, depart from us and take your prophet with you. We know he is a holy man, but the gods of our country do not know him, and we stand in danger of losing many swine.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said to Andrew, “⟦Q 151:6.7⟧Let us return to our place.⟦/Q⟧”
ch31.b031: As they were leaving, Amos begged to go with them, but the Master would not consent. “⟦Q 151:6.8⟧Forget not that you are a son of God. Return to your own people and show them what great things God has done for you.⟦/Q⟧” And Amos went through all the cities of the Decapolis, declaring what great things Jesus had done for him.
